reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / DeVita's Cancer: Principles & Practice of Oncology
clinicalPearls: Classified by anatomical site as intrahepatic, perihilar (Klatskin), or distal, and location strongly influences presentation, surgical approach, and outcome

Perihilar and distal tumours typically present with painless obstructive jaundice, pruritus, pale stools, and dark urine, whereas intrahepatic tumours often present later as a liver mass with vague abdominal pain or weight loss
Primary sclerosing cholangitis is a major predisposing condition, along with chronic biliary inflammation, liver fluke infestation in endemic regions, biliary tract stones, and choledochal cysts
CA 19-9 is a useful supportive marker but is neither sensitive nor specific and can be elevated by biliary obstruction or cholangitis alone
Tissue diagnosis and biliary anatomy are best defined with MRCP and, where needed, ERCP with brushings or cholangioscopy, taking care to avoid seeding and cholangitis
Only a minority of patients are candidates for curative resection, which may require major liver resection with biliary reconstruction depending on tumour location

For unresectable or metastatic disease, gemcitabine plus platinum chemotherapy is the systemic backbone, and molecular profiling for targetable alterations such as FGFR2 fusions and IDH1 mutations can guide targeted therapy
Relieving biliary obstruction with stenting is central to palliation and to controlling cholangitis and pruritus
reference.pathophysiology: Cholangiocarcinoma is a malignancy of the epithelial cells lining the intrahepatic or extrahepatic bile ducts, most often adenocarcinoma. Chronic inflammation and cholestasis, as seen in primary sclerosing cholangitis, chronic infection, or biliary stones, produce repeated epithelial injury and repair that promotes dysplasia and malignant transformation. The tumours are frequently desmoplastic and grow along the bile ducts, causing obstruction; perihilar lesions readily invade the portal structures and liver, while intrahepatic tumours behave as mass-forming liver cancers with early lymphatic and vascular spread.
additionalDifferentials: Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma causing distal biliary obstruction
Gallbladder carcinoma extending into the biliary tree
Hepatocellular carcinoma for intrahepatic mass lesions
Benign biliary stricture, including primary sclerosing cholangitis without malignancy
Metastatic adenocarcinoma to the liver or porta hepatis
additionalInvestigations: MRI with MRCP to map biliary anatomy and assess vascular and parenchymal involvement
Contrast-enhanced CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis for local staging and distant metastases
ERCP or percutaneous cholangiography with brush cytology or biopsy for tissue diagnosis and drainage
Serum CA 19-9 and CEA as supportive and monitoring markers
Molecular and genomic profiling of tumour tissue for FGFR2 fusions, IDH1 mutations, and other actionable targets
redFlags: Progressive painless obstructive jaundice with weight loss
Cholangitis with fever and rigors on a background of biliary stricture
New dominant biliary stricture in a patient with primary sclerosing cholangitis
Rapidly enlarging intrahepatic mass with vascular involvement on imaging
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally poor because most patients present with unresectable disease; complete resection with negative margins offers the best survival, while advanced disease treated with systemic therapy has limited long-term survival though molecularly targeted agents can extend it in selected patients.
pitfalls: Assuming obstructive jaundice is benign and delaying malignancy workup
Relying on a normal or mildly raised CA 19-9 to exclude cancer
Aggressive biliary instrumentation causing cholangitis before definitive staging
Missing a dominant malignant stricture within primary sclerosing cholangitis
references: DeVita's Cancer: Principles & Practice of Oncology
management: Confirm anatomic subtype (intrahepatic, perihilar, or distal) and discuss in a multidisciplinary hepatobiliary tumour board, since surgical options and staging diverge by subtype.
For resectable disease, surgery with an R0 margin is the only curative modality; staging laparoscopy is commonly used first to rule out occult peritoneal or distant spread.

Resection extent depends on subtype: nonanatomic to formal lobectomy for intrahepatic disease, hepatic lobectomy with extrahepatic bile duct and periportal lymphadenectomy for perihilar disease, and a pancreaticoduodenectomy-type approach for distal disease.

Consider liver transplantation only for carefully selected, early-stage unresectable perihilar tumours using a neoadjuvant chemoradiation plus staging laparoscopy protocol; transplantation is not routinely used for intrahepatic disease given poor results.

Offer adjuvant capecitabine after resection, which has shown a survival and recurrence-free survival benefit, while noting that trial evidence pools mixed biliary tract cancer populations; adjuvant gemcitabine-based regimens have not shown clear benefit.

For unresectable disease confined to the liver, consider local-regional therapies such as arterial embolization or ablation, and radiation therapy (including stereotactic approaches) for local control, recognizing limited randomized evidence.

Photodynamic therapy with biliary stenting may be considered at experienced centres for unresectable perihilar disease, but evidence is conflicting given a later trial showing shorter survival, so it should not be presented as an established survival benefit.
Use a platinum-gemcitabine doublet as first-line systemic therapy for advanced or metastatic disease, or enroll in a clinical trial.
Use a fluoropyrimidine-oxaliplatin combination as second-line therapy after progression on first-line gemcitabine-platinum therapy.

Pursue genomic profiling, especially for intrahepatic disease, to identify targetable alterations including FGFR2 fusions, IDH1 mutations, BRAF V600E, NTRK fusions, and HER2 amplification, and refer to a molecular tumour board or clinical trial for selective inhibitor therapy.

Provide biliary decompression via ERCP or PTC for obstructive jaundice or cholangitis regardless of resectability, and avoid EUS-FNA of a hilar lesion if transplantation is being considered due to tumour seeding risk.

Monitor after resection with liver function tests, CA 19-9, and cross-sectional imaging at roughly three-month intervals for the first two years and six-month intervals thereafter, since no formally validated surveillance guideline exists; a rising CA 19-9 may precede radiologic recurrence.
Refer patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis or choledochal cysts for ongoing surveillance given their markedly increased lifetime risk of cholangiocarcinoma.
